title: Reduced population density in urban deer following immunocontraceptive treatment trial
content:
These results indicate an apparent reduction in reproductive output and adult population density following 3 years of fertility control. However, the observed rebound in apparent fawn detections following reduced treatment effort in 2021—when fewer adult females received immunocontraceptive boosters and newly recruited does were not treated—suggests that effectiveness as an urban deer management strategy requires continued application, concurrent management of resource subsidies, and management of immigration from neighbouring populations.


Abstract

Human–wildlife conflict is an increasing concern in urban areas where proximity between people and wildlife leads to frequent interactions. While wildlife population management is often necessary in urban environments, lethal control methods are widely opposed by the public highlighting the need for effective non-lethal alternatives. We tested the efficacy of non-lethal immunocontraceptive treatment to reduce reproductive output in a population of black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) in Oak Bay, British Columbia. From 2019 to 2021, we treated 119 individual deer with immunocontraceptive, attached unique identifiers and used an array of camera traps deployed over 6 years (2018–2023), applying spatial mark-resight models to estimate adult population density for 1 year prior to treatment, during three consecutive treatment years and for 2 years post-treatment. Prior to immunocontraceptive treatment, the mean (±SD) number of independent detections with fawns was 19.1 ± 24.9 per site in 2018 and 16.8 ± 17.4 in 2019. Following initial immunocontraceptive treatment in 2019, detections with fawns dropped to 8.5 ± 12.4 in 2020 and 9.8 ± 11.2 in 2021. In the post-treatment period, detections with fawns increased to 16.5 ± 21.5 in 2022 and 14.4 ± 16.2 in 2023. Estimated adult deer density was 19.2 deer/km2 (95% CI: 16.4–22.5) in 2018 and 24.6 deer/km2 (95% CI: 21.4–28.3) in 2019, declining progressively to 20.9 deer/km2 (95% CI: 17.9–24.5) in 2020, 19.3 deer/km2 (95% CI: 16.3–22.9) in 2021, 14.8 deer/km2 (95% CI: 12.6–17.4) in 2022 and 13.7 deer/km2 (95% CI: 11.5–16.4) in 2023. Synthesis and applications. These results indicate an apparent reduction in reproductive output and adult population density following 3 years of fertility control. However, the observed rebound in apparent fawn detections following reduced treatment effort in 2021—when fewer adult females received immunocontraceptive boosters and newly recruited does were not treated—suggests that effectiveness as an urban deer management strategy requires continued application, concurrent management of resource subsidies and management of immigration from neighbouring populations.
